title: How to Set Up HTTP Redirects With Pangolin
summary: Send any hostname or path to another URL from the Pangolin dashboard. Attach redirects to a domain or a public resource, match on path, rewrite the path, and choose between temporary and permanent status codes.
body_markdown:
Pangolin 1.25 added redirects. A redirect takes a request for one URL and answers it with a` 307` or` 308` pointing the client somewhere else. You can use one to retire an old hostname, send the bare domain to` www` , move a section of a site to a new path, or route a single path on an existing resource to a different app.


Before redirects, doing this meant running a separate web server or editing proxy config by hand just to issue the hop. Now it is a form in the dashboard under **Settings > Redirects** , and the redirect is served by the same proxy that already fronts your resources.


This guide follows the walkthrough in the video below, then covers path matching, rewrites, and priority in more detail.


## Domain or Resource


Every redirect attaches to one of two things, and the choice decides which hostname it listens on.


A **domain-attached** redirect listens on a hostname built from one of your organization's[domains](https://docs.pangolin.net/manage/domains) plus an optional subdomain. Leave the subdomain empty to use the base domain itself. There does not need to be a resource on that hostname. Pangolin provisions a certificate for the host, and on self-hosted installs you can turn SSL off if you want plain HTTP. On Pangolin Cloud, HTTPS is always on. Deleting the domain deletes its redirects, but deleting or disabling a resource on the same hostname leaves the redirect alone.


A **resource-attached** redirect listens on the full hostname of an existing[public resource](https://docs.pangolin.net/manage/resources/public/http-https) , including wildcards if the resource uses them. TLS follows the resource. Requests that match the redirect get sent away, and every other request goes to the resource as usual. If the resource is disabled or has no domain, the redirect is inactive, and if the resource is deleted, the redirect goes with it.


Pick a domain when the hostname has nothing behind it, or when you want the redirect to outlive whatever resource happens to be on that host. Pick a resource when you want a few paths on a live app to go somewhere else.


## Step by Step


The video starts from an empty organization so there is something to redirect to. If you already have a working resource, skip to step 3.


### 1. Create a site and a test app


Go to the **Sites** tab, click **Add Site** , and give it a name like` test-redirect` . Pangolin shows a command to start the site connector. Copy it, click **Create Site** , and run the command on the machine you want to expose. In the video this is a laptop.


On the same machine, start something to look at. The video uses a small HTTP server on` localhost:8000` that prints back the request and its headers, which makes it easy to see what arrived after a redirect. Any local web server works.


### 2. Create a public resource


Go to **Resources** and click **Add Resource** . Choose **HTTP** , name it` test` , set the subdomain to` test` , and add a target on the` test-redirect` site pointing at` localhost:8000` . After you create it,` test.example.com` loads the same page as` localhost:8000` , with a few extra headers added by the proxy.


### 3. Redirect a hostname to another URL


Go to **Redirects** and click **Add Redirect** . Name it` redirect-one` and leave it enabled.


Attach it to a **Domain** , pick your domain, and enter` redirect` as the subdomain. For the destination, enter any origin. The video uses an external site to show that the destination can be anywhere:


Field Value


Attach to Domain


Subdomain` redirect`


Destination` https://example.org`


Match path (empty)


Leave the match path empty so every request to` redirect.example.com` is redirected. Save it, open` redirect.example.com` in a browser, and you land on` example.org` .


To point the same hostname at your own resource instead, open the redirect again, change the destination to` https://test.example.com` , and click **Save Settings** . The next visit to` redirect.example.com` ends up at the test app.


### 4. Redirect one path on a resource


Create a second redirect called` redirect-two` . This time attach it to a **Resource** and choose` test` .


Since the resource already serves the whole hostname, you usually want to match a path here rather than everything. Say all of` test.example.com` should stay on the test app except` /api` , which should go elsewhere:


Field Value


Attach to Resource (` test` )


Path match type Prefix


Match path` /api`


Destination` https://example.org`


Now` test.example.com/` still loads the app. A request to` test.example.com/api/v1` is redirected to` https://example.org/api/v1` . The path came along because, by default, Pangolin keeps the original path and query string and only swaps the origin.


### 5. Check the logs


Redirects show up in the same request logs as resources. Go to **Logs & Analytics** and open **HTTP Request Logs** . Each row shows who made the request, why it was allowed, and where it went, so the` /api/v1` request from step 4 appears with its redirect target next to it.


## How Matching Works


A request matches a redirect when its` Host` header equals the redirect's listen host and its path matches the redirect's path rule. A redirect with no path rule matches every path on the host.


Match type What matches


Exact The path equals the match path


Prefix The path starts with the match path as a whole segment, so` /products` matches` /products/shoes` but not` /productsforsale`


Regex The path matches the regular expression


When a redirect and a resource share a hostname, Pangolin checks the redirect first. This includes checking it before the resource's authentication, so a visitor who hits a matching path is redirected without being asked to log in. That is useful for sending a public path like` /status` to a status page, but keep it in mind before attaching a broad redirect to a protected resource.


## Rewriting the Path


The destination field takes an origin only: scheme, host, and an optional port, such as` https://example.com` or` https://example.com:8443` . Paths, query strings, and fragments do not go in that field. The URL the client receives is built like this:


```text
destination origin + rewritten path + original query string


```


With no rewrite set, the rewritten path is the original path. To change it, choose a rewrite type:


Rewrite type Effect


Exact Replace the whole path with a fixed one


Prefix Replace the matched prefix and keep the rest


Regex Substitute using the match pattern, with` $1` ,` $2` for groups


Strip prefix Remove the matched prefix, and optionally add a new one


If you only want to change the path and keep visitors on the same host, set the destination to **Same Domain as Source** .


A few examples:


To move a section of a site, take a resource at` docs.example.com` , match on prefix` /guides` , rewrite with type Prefix to` /tutorials` , and use Same Domain as Source.` /guides/install` becomes` /tutorials/install` .


To split an old path onto its own host, use` app.example.com` , match prefix` /legacy` , set the destination to` https://legacy.example.com` , and strip the prefix.` /legacy/reports?id=4` becomes` https://legacy.example.com/reports?id=4` .


Regex on both sides can reorder parts of a URL. This one moves` /blog/2020/post` to` /archive/post-2020` :


Field Value


Path match type Regex


Match path` ^/blog/(\\d+)/(.*)$`


Rewrite type Regex


Rewrite path` /archive/$2-$1`


Substitution follows the same rules as JavaScript's` String.replace` . If you pair a Prefix match with a Regex rewrite, whatever comes after the prefix is available as` $1` , so matching` /old` and rewriting to` /new$1` turns` /old/x` into` /new/x` .


## Temporary or Permanent


Redirects are temporary by default and return` 307` . Browsers do not hold on to a` 307` , so you can change the destination later and visitors pick up the change right away.


Turn on **Permanent** to return` 308` instead. Browsers and search engines may cache a` 308` and stop asking, which is what you want for a hostname you have retired for good, and a problem if you change your mind. Use temporary while testing and switch once the destination is settled.


Both codes keep the original request method, so a` POST` to the old URL is still a` POST` at the new one.


On self-hosted installs, permanent redirects need Badger v1.8.0 or newer. The 1.25 migration updates Badger when it finds the Traefik config in the standard location. Otherwise, update it by hand.


## Priority


Each redirect has a priority from 1 to 1000, and higher numbers are checked first. Redirects always sit in front of resources on the same host regardless of the number, so priority only matters when two or more redirects could match the same request. For example, give an exact match on` /api/health` a higher priority than a prefix match on` /api` so the health check goes to its own destination.


## FAQ


**Do I need a resource or a site to create a redirect?**


*Not for a domain-attached redirect. It listens on a hostname from one of your domains whether or not a resource uses it. The video creates a site and resource only so there is a local app to redirect to. Resource-attached redirects need an existing public resource with a domain.*


**Does a redirect on a protected resource skip authentication?**


*For requests that match it, yes. Pangolin evaluates redirects before resource authentication, so a matching request is redirected without a login prompt. Requests that do not match the redirect still go through the resource's normal authentication.*


**Is the query string kept?**


*Yes. The original query string is always appended to the final URL, after any path rewrite.*


**Can I put a path in the destination?**


*No. The destination is an origin only. Use a path rewrite (Exact, Prefix, Regex, or Strip prefix) to control the path on the other side.*


**What status codes does Pangolin return?**


*` 307` for temporary redirects and` 308` for permanent ones. Both preserve the HTTP method and body.*


**How do I redirect the bare domain to www?**


*Create a domain-attached redirect on your base domain with the subdomain left empty, leave the match path empty, and set the destination to` https://www.example.com` . The path and query string carry over unchanged. Turn on Permanent once you have confirmed it works.*


**Can I see which requests were redirected?**


*Yes. Redirected requests appear in **Logs & Analytics > HTTP Request Logs** alongside resource requests, with the destination they were sent to.*


**Is Pangolin open source?**


*Yes. Pangolin is open source and self-hostable. You can deploy the whole platform yourself, use[Pangolin Cloud](https://app.pangolin.net/auth/signup) , or mix hosted and self-hosted components. Redirects are available in both.*
